Let \(L\) be the set of uncovered triples of \(V\), i.e. the \(3\)-subsets not contained in any block of \(\mathcal B\). If \(r_x\) is the number of blocks containing \(x\), then the number of uncovered triples containing \(x\) is

\[
d_x=\binom{10}{2}-3r_x=45-3r_x.
\]

Since \(r_x\) is even, \(d_x\equiv 3\pmod 6\).

For a fixed pair \(\{x,y\}\), there are \(9\) triples containing it. Each block containing \(\{x,y\}\) covers exactly two of those triples, so an odd number of them remain uncovered. In particular, every pair lies in at least one uncovered triple. Thus, for each \(x\),

\[
2d_x=\sum_{y\ne x} \#\{\text{uncovered triples containing }x,y\}\ge 10.
\]

Together with \(d_x\equiv 3\pmod 6\), this gives \(d_x\ge 9\). Hence

\[
3|L|=\sum_x d_x\ge 11\cdot 9=99,
\]

so \(|L|\ge 33\). Since each block covers \(4\) triples,

\[
4|\mathcal B|=165-|L|\le 132,
\]

so

\[
|\mathcal B|\le 33.
\]

This bound is attainable. Take \(V=\mathbb Z_{11}\) and all translates of

\[
\{0,1,2,4\},\qquad \{0,1,5,7\},\qquad \{0,1,6,9\}.
\]

Their twelve internal triples represent distinct translation classes, so no triple is repeated. Each point occurs \(4\) times in each translate-orbit, hence \(12\) times total, which is even. Therefore the maximum possible cardinality is \(33\).

Now suppose \(|\mathcal B|=33\). Then equality above forces \(d_x=9\) and \(r_x=12\) for every \(x\).

Let \(n_i\) be the number of unordered pairs of distinct blocks intersecting in exactly \(i\) points. Since no two blocks share \(3\) points, only \(i=0,1,2\) occur. We want \(n_0\).

We have

\[
n_1+2n_2=\sum_x \binom{r_x}{2}
=11\binom{12}{2}=726,
\]

and

\[
n_0+n_1+n_2=\binom{33}{2}=528.
\]

Thus

\[
n_0=n_2-198.
\]

For a pair \(\{x,y\}\), write \(l_{xy}\) for the number of uncovered triples containing it. Then \(l_{xy}\) is positive and odd, so write

\[
l_{xy}=1+2b_{xy}.
\]

Since \(d_x=9\),

\[
\sum_{y\ne x} l_{xy}=18,
\]

so

\[
\sum_{y\ne x} b_{xy}=4.
\]

Therefore

\[
\sum_{\{x,y\}} b_{xy}=22.
\]

The number \(\lambda_{xy}\) of blocks containing \(\{x,y\}\) is

\[
\lambda_{xy}=\frac{9-l_{xy}}2=4-b_{xy}.
\]

Hence

\[
n_2=\sum_{\{x,y\}}\binom{\lambda_{xy}}2
=\sum_{\{x,y\}}\binom{4-b_{xy}}2.
\]

For \(b=0,1,2,3,4\),

\[
\binom{4-b}{2}\ge 6-3b.
\]

Thus

\[
n_2\ge 55\cdot 6-3\cdot 22=264,
\]

so

\[
n_0\ge 264-198=66.
\]

The cyclic construction above attains equality: its pair multiplicities are \(4,4,3,3,4\) by cyclic distance \(1,2,3,4,5\), so exactly the equality case occurs. Therefore the minimum possible number of disjoint block pairs among maximum-size families is

\[
\boxed{66}.
\]
